frameworks.name: FCB grid (Vaughn 1980, Foote Cone & Belding)
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: The purchase decision, not the industry. Two axes: involvement (high/low) and think/feel (cognitive vs affective). Four quadrants: informative (high/think, e.g. cars, insurance), affective (high/feel, e.g. jewellery, fashion), habitual (low/think, e.g. household staples), self-satisfaction (low/feel, e.g. snacks, beer). Each quadrant gets its own learn-feel-do sequence and creative approach.
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Widely taught and used for planning. Ratchford (1987, JAR 27(4)) placed 60 products on the grid with survey data and found involvement and think/feel are correlated: a decision that is high on thinking or feeling tends to be high-involvement. Later studies had to revisit where categories sit for online shopping (2020 update), and a 2022 paper revisits it for social media. Two practical lessons: placement belongs to a product or decision, and it moves over time. Products inside one industry can land in different quadrants, e.g. a budget rental and a luxury chalet are both real estate.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: Several rule types in our L2 'sector overlay' (tone and register, format lead, proof) are really set by the decision type, not the sector. A luxury real-estate client (N°3 Courchevel) and a mass-market one share compliance rules but not appeal or tone. Add a small 'decision profile' facet (about 4 values: involvement x think/feel), set per client or per product line at onboarding, rather than inferring it from industry.

frameworks.name: Rossiter-Percy grid (Rossiter, Percy & Bellman)
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: Brand purchase risk (low/high involvement) x purchase motivation: informational (negative motives such as problem removal or avoidance) vs transformational (positive motives: sensory gratification, social approval). Unlike FCB it also gives separate tactics for brand awareness (recognition vs recall).
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Common in marketing-communications teaching and in planning practice. The empirical support is mixed. In an experiment, Loef, Antonides & van Raaij found ads that MISMATCH the motivation beat matching ones on brand and ad evaluations, explained by schema-incongruity theory. So 'match appeal to motive' is a prior, not a law.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: Supports the same decision-profile facet as FCB, with motivation (informational vs transformational) as the more useful axis for social copy: problem/solution carousels vs aspiration and sensory Reels. Because the matching rule failed an experimental test, make it a DEFAULT that L3 performance data can override, never a hard rule. It also suggests a deliberate small share of 'counter-type' posts, which fits the L3 promotion ladder.

frameworks.name: Ehrenberg-Bass: category entry points (CEPs), distinctive brand assets (DBAs), and 'brand user profiles seldom differ'
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: CEPs are specific to a CATEGORY: the situations, needs, moods and times that make buyers think of it (e.g. 'Friday night out' for music events, 'planning a ski week' for chalets). DBAs are specific to a BRAND: colours, logo, characters, sounds. Hammond, Ehrenberg & Goodhardt (1996) found that competing brands in a category are bought by near-identical kinds of people.
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Romaniuk's CEP and DBA measures (Building Distinctive Brand Assets, 2018; Better Brand Health) are standard at large advertisers. Hammond et al. used a year of panel data across 23 grocery categories in the US, UK, Germany and Japan and found little brand segmentation. Dawes's 95:5 out-of-market finding comes from the same institute.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: This is the strongest argument for keeping a CATEGORY unit in the middle layer. CEPs, the buyer calendar and the category's visual conventions are shared by every brand in the category, so they belong in L2. Brand distinctiveness (the DBAs: kit logo, palette, recurring characters and formats) belongs in L3, never L2. Buyers don't split by brand inside a category, so L2 should not try to encode an 'audience type' by brand positioning. Concrete step: each category pack carries a CEP list for posts to anchor to. The CEP list is worth more than engagement benchmarks.

frameworks.name: Binet & Field: The Long and the Short of It (2013) and Effectiveness in Context (2018)
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: Brand-building vs sales-activation balance, moderated by the kind of consideration: high vs low, and emotional vs rational. Market type (online-first, B2B, services, durables) shifts the optimal split.
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: IPA Databank of 996 campaigns (1980-2010), later expanded. The about-60:40 brand:activation optimum shifts to about 50:50 for online-first brands and B2B. Brand effects are easier where emotional consideration is high and activation effects where rational consideration is high. High-consideration categories get bigger effects per extra unit of share of voice.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: Emotional/rational consideration is a better predictor of what works than the industry label. It maps onto the decision-profile facet. That facet should set the default mix of brand-personality (emotional, entertaining) posts vs activation (offer, CTA, informative) posts, and L3 tunes it. Commercial model (B2B, online-first, local footfall) is a second modifier on that mix.

frameworks.name: B2B vs B2C: LinkedIn B2B Institute, Google/CEB, Swani et al.
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: Commercial model (business buyers vs consumers), and the share of buyers in or out of market (95:5).
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Binet & Field's B2B cut of the IPA data for the B2B Institute (2019) found emotion is almost as important in B2B as in B2C: emotional ads win long-term, rational ones short-term, about 50:50 brand/activation. The Google/CEB survey (3,000 buyers of 36 B2B brands) found personal value has about 2x the impact of business value, and B2B buyers are more emotionally attached to brands than B2C buyers. Dawes (Ehrenberg-Bass): about 5% of B2B buyers are in market at any time. Swani, Brown & Milne content-analysed Fortune 500 posts: B2B firms in practice use more corporate brand names, more functional appeals and more links. Swani, Milne et al. found that corporate names, functional AND emotional appeals, and info-search cues all raise B2B message effectiveness. So practice differs more than effectiveness does.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: B2B vs B2C should NOT be a top-level split with different tone rules. The evidence says emotional, memorable creative works in both. B2B is a light modifier: named-company and people-led proof, longer-cycle calendar, about 50:50 mix, link and info cues allowed. It should not replace the decision-profile facet. Karos's own account and Geektime's B2B side would get the modifier, not a separate rulebook.

frameworks.name: Social-post content research (Lee, Hosanagar & Nair 2018; de Vries, Gensler & Leeflang 2012)
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: Content characteristics, not industry: brand-personality content (humour, emotion, chit-chat) vs directly informative content (deals, product info). Also vividness (image, video) and interactivity (questions, quizzes).
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Lee et al. (Management Science 64(11)): 106,316 Facebook posts from 782 companies, coded with MTurk + NLP. Brand-personality content raises likes, comments and shares; informative content such as deals raises click-throughs. They recommend combining the two. De Vries et al. (J. Interactive Marketing, 355 posts, 11 brands, 6 categories): questions raise comments, vividness has mixed effects, and top-of-page placement helps.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: These effects held across hundreds of companies in many industries, so they belong in L1 as defaults: always blend personality and informative posts, and use questions to draw comments. What varies by client is the weighting, which the decision profile and objective set and L3 then learns. Evidence that a rule holds across industries is a reason to keep it out of L2 and stop L2 from growing.

frameworks.name: Content typologies: Hero/Hub/Help (YouTube/Google 2015) and the Content Marketing Matrix (Smart Insights/First 10: entertain, inspire, educate, convince)
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: The job a piece of content does and its cadence: tent-pole 'hero' moments, recurring 'hub' series, search-driven 'help'. The matrix crosses emotional vs rational with awareness vs purchase.
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Practitioner frameworks with no controlled evidence behind them. They are used almost everywhere as planning and audit tools. Google's 2015 YouTube playbook made hero/hub/help standard vocabulary. The matrix is used to audit a content mix.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: These frameworks work in every vertical, so they are not candidates for the middle layer. They describe the mix of post jobs in a calendar. Treat 'post job' (hero/hub/help, or entertain/inspire/educate/convince) as a run-level or calendar-level PARAMETER on each post. Default weights come from the decision profile and objective, and actual weights are learned in L3. Recurring 'hub' series are also the natural home for a client's distinctive formats (DBAs in format form).

frameworks.name: Account archetype: creator vs business accounts on Instagram, Meta Page types, brand vs creator vs publisher behaviour
frameworks.what_it_segments_by: WHO is speaking. Instagram splits accounts into personal, creator and business, with different features: creator accounts get the full music library, while business accounts get only commercially licensed audio but full ads and API access. Meta's Page taxonomy starts with six types: Local Business or Place; Company, Organization or Institution; Brand or Product; Artist, Band or Public Figure; Entertainment; Cause or Community. Under those sit about 1,300-1,400 specific categories.
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: The platform itself uses this two-tier taxonomy. Dash Social data (small n=116 campaigns) shows creator-led content lifts average engagement while brand content dominates the top quartile. The Sprout Social Index 2025 says consumers reward original, human, behind-the-scenes content from brands. Rival IQ's 14 benchmark 'industries' include 'Influencers' and 'Media', which shows that practice mixes account type into industry lists.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: This is a separate axis from industry, and it drives voice, first-person vs brand-plural, face-on-camera, audio availability (a hard platform constraint), cadence and the UGC-vs-produced look. Our clients show it clearly: Don Techno and Inspiration Music are artist or label accounts, N°3 Courchevel is a local place, Geektime is a publisher, Karos is a B2B company. An industry-only L2 would mix up a DJ and a nightclub, which share an industry but not a voice. Add an 'account archetype' facet with about 6 values based on Meta's top tier. It needs few values, is stable, and is known at onboarding.

frameworks.name: Industry benchmarks and vertical playbooks (Rival IQ, Meta creative guidance, specialist agencies)
frameworks.evidence_or_adoption: Rival IQ 2025 covers 14 industries and 2,100 brands. Instagram median engagement is about 0.36%, and only Higher Ed and Sports Teams exceed 1%, which shows real between-industry spread. Meta runs creative studies by vertical (e-commerce, CPG, retail, professional services), but its core Reels guidance (9:16, sound on, human presence, a hook in the first seconds) is the same for all verticals. Specialist agencies (e.g. SaaS-only shops) sell vertical playbooks and benchmarks. Nielsen's 2017 analysis of about 500 campaigns attributes about 47% of sales lift to creative quality, vs 15% to brand and 9% to targeting.
frameworks.implication_for_our_layers: Industry really owns compliance and claims (finance, health, alcohol), benchmark baselines, buyer calendar and proof conventions. It does not own the creative craft rules, which platforms publish as the same for every vertical (L1). Keep a 'category pack' but narrow it to what the evidence says varies by category: hard compliance rules, CEPs, calendar, proof types, visual conventions and benchmark baselines. Tone and format lead move to the archetype and decision-profile facets.

practice: Platforms classify accounts on two tiers: a small set of account or page TYPES, then a long list of CATEGORIES. Meta has six page types (Local Business/Place; Company/Organization; Brand/Product; Artist/Band/Public Figure; Entertainment; Cause/Community) with about 1,300-1,400 categories beneath them, and a page picks up to 3. Instagram adds personal / creator / business account types with different features, e.g. music-library access.

Benchmark vendors report by industry: Rival IQ uses 14 industries (Alcohol, Fashion, Financial Services, F&B, Health & Beauty, Higher Ed, Home Decor, Influencers, Media, Nonprofits, Retail, Sports Teams, Tech & Software, Travel). They slip account types ('Influencers', 'Media') into the industry list, so practice mixes 'who speaks' with 'what category' without saying so.

Specialist agencies sell vertical playbooks (SaaS-only, hospitality, healthcare), mainly for benchmarks, compliance and buyer-journey knowledge. Generalist agencies and platform creative teams (Meta Reels guidance, YouTube hero/hub/help) publish creative craft rules that are the same across verticals.

Content planning inside agencies runs on frameworks that ignore vertical: content pillars per client, hero/hub/help cadence, and the entertain/inspire/educate/convince audit matrix. Vertical knowledge changes topics, calendar and proof; the framework for the post mix stays the same.

Strategy planners choose creative approach by decision type (FCB grid, Rossiter-Percy) and by brand vs activation balance (Binet & Field), not by industry label. Products in one industry often sit in different quadrants.

Ehrenberg-Bass-influenced teams build category-level CEP maps shared by all brands in the category, and keep brand-level work for distinctive assets. That split matches our L2 (category knowledge) and L3 (the client's distinctive assets and learned performance).

B2B social practice in the field is more functional and link-heavy than B2C (Swani et al.). The effectiveness evidence (Binet & Field for the B2B Institute; Google/CEB) says B2B should use MORE emotion than it does. Industry practice is therefore a weak guide to what works.
research.recommendation_from_literature:
Keep three layers, but stop treating L2 as one 'industry' axis. Make L2 a composed overlay of three small facets. Each facet OWNS a fixed set of rule types, so the facets never compete on one rule type and need no precedence order between them. Don't add a fourth stacked layer.

(1) CATEGORY PACK: the industry/category, open-ended and grown per client. Owns hard compliance and claims rules, category entry points (CEPs), buyer calendar, proof conventions, visual conventions of the category and benchmark baselines. Basis: Ehrenberg-Bass says CEPs are category-level and brand user profiles within a category barely differ. Compliance is industry-specific by law. Rival IQ benchmarks vary by industry.

(2) ACCOUNT ARCHETYPE, about 6 values from Meta's top-tier page types: brand/product, local business/place, artist/creator/public figure, publisher/media, B2B company/institution, cause/community. Owns voice person (I/we/brand), face-on-camera and UGC-vs-produced look, audio availability (a hard platform constraint for business vs creator accounts), cadence, and collab/mention behaviour. Basis: Instagram and Meta themselves split on this axis, and a DJ and a nightclub share an industry but not a voice.

(3) DECISION PROFILE, about 4 values: involvement x think/feel, or equivalently Binet & Field's emotional vs rational consideration. Owns the default appeal mix (informational vs transformational), tone register, format lead, and the brand-personality vs activation weighting of the calendar (about 60:40, shifted to about 50:50 for B2B or online-first). Basis: FCB, Rossiter-Percy, and Effectiveness in Context. It is set per client or per product line at onboarding, never inferred from industry.

B2B vs B2C is a light modifier (named-company and people-led proof, longer calendar, about 50:50 mix), not a separate branch. The evidence says emotion works in B2B too.

Rules that held across hundreds of companies stay in L1 as defaults: blend brand-personality and informative content (Lee, Hosanagar & Nair; 782 firms), use questions to drive comments, and follow native Reels craft.

'Post job' (hero/hub/help, or entertain/inspire/educate/convince) is a per-post or per-calendar parameter whose default weights come from the decision profile and whose actual weights L3 learns. It is not a layer.

Brand distinctiveness (the kit logo, palette, recurring formats and characters, i.e. the DBAs) stays in L3.

Four reasons to prefer facets over a single sector:
(a) The current L2 rule types (proof, compliance, tone, format lead, timing, hashtag tolerance, visual style, buyer calendar) turn out to come from different axes in the literature.
(b) Cross-client learning pools better. The 'wins in ≥2 clients becomes an L2 default' promotion rule fires far more often on a 6-value archetype or 4-value decision profile than on fine-grained sectors with one or two Karos clients each.
(c) A new client can be classified at onboarding with three quick picks, even in a category Karos has never served.
(d) The rules that fail empirical tests, such as Rossiter-Percy matching (Loef et al. found mismatching ads won), stay overridable defaults rather than hard rules.

Caveats: the FCB and Rossiter-Percy grids are planning heuristics with mixed experimental support, and most social-content evidence measures engagement, not sales. Treat facet defaults as priors that L3 performance data is expected to overturn, and log every override so the facet defaults themselves get reviewed.

verdict.what_the_data_says: Plainly: no grouping of the 89 benchmark accounts predicts how posting patterns behave better than pooling everyone. 15 of 16 groupings have negative skill at k=3, meaning "predict this account from its group" is worse than "predict it from all other accounts". The one positive, involvement (+0.0028, 3 groups of 27-31), is a 0.3% error reduction, at the floor of what 199 shuffles can resolve, and would vanish under a slightly different k. Industry (-0.0148) and vertical (-0.0256) are among the worst; every crossed grouping (13-22 cells) is worse than either parent; locale is indistinguishable from shuffled labels (perm_p 0.51). The low perm_p on negative-skill groupings (archetype, industry, archetype x involvement, all 0.005) says the real labels DO carry structure, but at 6-30 accounts per group the grouped estimate is noisier than the global one and k=3 does not shrink enough to rescue it. Two confounds cap what can be concluded: industry is nearly identical to source client (each industry is one client's competitor set, 6 of 7 with exactly one Karos client), and locale is nested inside industry (all he = Hebrew tech news, all pt-BR = Brazilian fintech), so vertical and locale effects cannot be separated from sampling. The outcome is within-account engagement share (best-minus-weakest), not reach, clicks or sales. Conclusion: L1 (global pool, one vote per account) and L3 (the client's own posts, shrunk toward global) carry essentially all the performance weight today. The middle layer earns its place only as authored knowledge and mechanics (compliance, entry points, calendar, voice, audio, mix defaults from the literature), not as a pool of engagement evidence. Involvement is the only facet worth watching for future pattern deltas; archetype is second (-0.0037, the fewest-levels loser).

scores.design: One middle layer: the Stakes band (involvement, 3 values)
scores.comment: Picks the only grouping that beat global and the coarsest one, so its pooling is the most defensible of the three that pool at all. But it still promotes +0.0028 into a real evidence-pooling layer, which the size of the effect does not justify, and its perm_p ceiling (0.005) is the test's floor. Research fit is weaker: it demotes archetype to a descriptive tag, so voice person, face-on-camera and the hard audio constraint (business vs creator account) have no owner except L3, and Meta's own account split, the DJ-vs-nightclub argument, is lost. Its 3-step classification question is the best of the three and should be kept. Tailoring is thin: Hanky Panky and Kindly Yours and Sitti collapse to one band plus a kit, and all differentiation falls to L3.

scores.design: Two-axis middle: Client Type (L2a) under Vertical Field (L2b), composed by field ownership
scores.comment: Right instincts: vertical holds NO performance deltas, only involvement may, and only when gated by a re-run of the predictive test plus a 2-client win. The field-ownership table with a lint is the correct answer to 'which facet wins'. Ordering L2a below L2b is well argued but is precedence machinery the design itself makes unnecessary once keys have single owners. Six onboarding picks, three card families, seven vertical packs and locale sheets is a lot of surface for a middle layer that carries no evidence yet. Still lets involvement carry deltas on a +0.0028 result, which is generous. Client mapping is the most careful of the three and its coverage check (every involvement cell has 2+ clients) is useful.

scores.design: Facet Packs: small parameter packs, each owning its own keys, over one globally pooled evidence base
scores.comment: The most honest reading of the numbers: performance learning is global (L1) and per client (L3) with nothing in between; facets hold standards only until a facet passes an explicit skill gate on two consecutive storms. The provenance map and 'category pack supplies values to an L1 gate' keep the middleware's L1-only-hard rule intact. Research fit is complete (archetype, category, decision profile, audience as a 2-key modifier, Loef counter-type share). Costs: a 3x2 decision table adds an untested motive axis the benchmark never tagged, per-product-line profiles add a run-input dependency, and a registry plus CI plus compileDNA is real engineering before any client benefits. Its 0.02 skill gate is stricter than the evidence base can plausibly reach at 89 accounts, so it should be recalibrated rather than copied. Placing Hanky Panky in high involvement is the one mapping I would reverse.

recommended.name: Thin middle: three standards-only facet cards over one global pool (Design 3's evidence rule, Design 2's closed lists and ownership table, Design 1's classification question)
recommended.layers:
L1 PLATFORM: Instagram craft prompts, code gates (mechanism half of every hard rule), and ALL pooled performance defaults, learned across every benchmark account with one vote per account. The only layer besides L3 that may state 'X lifts engagement'.
L2 FACETS (merged side by side, never stacked, each owns disjoint parameter keys, all hold STANDARDS only, no engagement claims):
  L2a ARCHETYPE, closed list of 7: owns voice person, face-on-camera, produced-vs-UGC look, audio source (hard, read from the IG account type via API), cadence default, collab/mention style, news-peg handling, series affinity.
  L2b CATEGORY PACK, open list, one per field served: owns compliance and claims values (per jurisdiction key, fed to the L1 claims gate), 8-15 category entry points, buyer/cultural calendar, proof conventions, lingo and topic bank, imagery source (replaces PHOTO_FIRST_INDUSTRY and the visual_dependency tag), category visual conventions, benchmark peer set and reporting baselines.
  L2c INVOLVEMENT, closed list of 3: owns default post-job mix (entertain/inspire/educate/convince), brand-vs-activation ratio (60:40 default), CTA intensity default, register intensity, format lead. Plus an AUDIENCE MODIFIER (B2B/B2C/mixed) that may shift exactly two keys: brand_vs_activation_ratio (toward 50:50) and proof_person_style (named company or person).
QUALIFIERS (not layers, never pool evidence): LOCALE (en, he, pt-BR, es, fr, multi) owns script direction, register pack, number/date/currency format and the jurisdiction key; resolved exact locale, then base language, then default. SIZE has no rules; used only to pick benchmark peers and normalise baselines.
L3 CLIENT DNA, one per client: distinctive brand assets (kit logo byte for byte, palette, fonts, recurring series and characters), positioning inside the category (premium vs value), appeal lean (informational vs transformational, an untested prior kept here rather than as a facet), forbidden topics, overrides of any non-hard L2 key each with a reason, learned performance weights shrunk toward L1 global (never toward a facet), and the promotion ladder.
RUN INPUT: post job and product line (product line may override involvement only).
Precedence, highest first: L1 hard gates > run input > L3 DNA > L2 facets (no order among them, keys never overlap) > L1 defaults. compileDNA(client, run) is a pure function at dispatch with a provenance map per key; no model call at run time.
recommended.taxonomy:
ARCHETYPE (closed, 7; Meta top-tier page types merged with the benchmark coding; 'educator/advisor' folds into person until it has 5+ benchmark accounts):
- brand: consumer product brand
- place: local business, venue, property (N°3 Courchevel)
- person: creator, artist, personality, educator or advisor posting in a first-person human voice
- publisher: media, news or curation page with an editorial 'we' or faceless voice
- platform: consumer app, software, marketplace
- business: B2B company, agency or service
- institution: program, event, competition, community or cause
Tie-break: pick the voice the account actually posts in (first-person human = person; editorial/curatorial = publisher).
INVOLVEMENT (closed, 3; same labels as the benchmark tags so client and evidence share one definition):
- none: content is the product; the account earns from attention (sponsorship, ads, tickets, plays)
- low: the viewer can act within minutes, typical order or commitment under about $100/EUR 100, nothing regulated
- high: acting takes research, money or commitment, or the category is regulated (finance, health, alcohol, legal, real estate), or it is a B2B contract, or an application/program costing days of effort
AUDIENCE MODIFIER (closed, 3): B2B, B2C, mixed. No rulebook of its own; two keys only.
CATEGORY PACK (open, seeded from the benchmark): marketing-advertising, tech-business-news, startups-venture, fashion-intimates, travel-local-discovery, personal-finance-investing, music-nightlife; grows one pack per new field (luxury-hospitality-real-estate next). 'other' is not a valid final value; a stub pack is opened instead. 'Industry' survives only as a free-text label on the client, never a key.
LOCALE (closed ISO-style list): en, he, pt-BR, es, fr, multi. Owns language mechanics and the jurisdiction key only.
DESCRIPTIVE TAGS (recorded on clients and benchmark accounts, select no rules): content_job, visual_dependency, size, industry, motive lean.
DEFINITIONS: a STANDARD is a convention or constraint that claims no engagement lift; only L2 holds standards. A PERFORMANCE CLAIM says a recipe level lifts engagement; only L1 (global) and L3 (per client) may hold one unless a facet has passed the skill gate. POST JOB is a per-run parameter, not a layer. Every parameter key has exactly one owner in facet-registry.json; CI fails on two owners or on a pack writing a key it does not own.
recommended.client_mapping:
Fields: archetype | category pack | involvement | audience | locale (jurisdiction).
- karoslabs: business | marketing-advertising | high | B2B (mix to 50:50, named-company and people-led proof) | en
- geektime: publisher | tech-business-news | none | mixed (readers B2C, advertisers and events B2B; events campaigns may take a per-run high override, logged) | he (RTL, Hebrew register pack)
- thepitchbydeel: institution | startups-venture | high (applying is a selective, weeks-of-effort decision) | mixed (founders and investors) | en
- hankypanky: brand | fashion-intimates | low (borderline: premium but typical order under about $100, repeat and affective; rationale logged, re-check if AOV crosses the line) | B2C | en. Appeal lean transformational and premium positioning live in L3 DNA.
- kindlyyours: brand | fashion-intimates | low | B2C | en. Identical L2 stack to hankypanky on purpose (Ehrenberg-Bass: buyers inside a category barely differ); value positioning and size-inclusive voice live in L3.
- sitti: platform (two-sided marketplace; publisher is the neighbouring row and shares voice_person) | travel-local-discovery | low (free app install) | mixed (creators and map users) | en
- xodigital: platform (tokenised offerings; app is the neighbouring row) | personal-finance-investing | high (regulated investing) | B2C | pt-BR (jurisdiction BR selects the CVM claims list in the category pack, fed to the L1 claims gate)
- dontechno: publisher (person is the alternative if it is run as one DJ's voice; audio source follows the IG account type) | music-nightlife | none | B2C | en
Coverage: every involvement value has at least 2 Karos clients (high 3, low 3, none 2); only fashion-intimates has 2 clients at the category level, which is one more reason category packs never learn performance. N°3 Courchevel would enter as place | luxury-hospitality-real-estate (new pack) | high | B2C | fr; Inspiration Music as person | music-nightlife | none | B2C | en.
recommended.how_a_client_is_classified:
Once, at onboarding, inside the existing onboarding research step; no model calls at run time.
1. One haiku-class call reads the client profile, website, IG bio and last 12 posts and proposes archetype, category, involvement, audience and locale, each with a one-line reason. Locale comes from detected caption language.
2. The IG account type (business vs creator) is read from the API as a fact and sets audio_source.
3. Involvement is decided by the three-question rule (Design 1's), applied to the PRIMARY revenue line the feed is asked to convert: (a) is the posting itself what the audience comes for, with money following from attention? then none; (b) otherwise, does acting require research, money or commitment: regulated category, or a typical order/commitment above about $100, or a B2B contract, or an application costing days of effort? then high; (c) otherwise low. Benchmark accounts are tagged with the same three questions.
4. Staff confirm or change the five picks on the client settings page. Stored on the Client as classification: {archetype, category, involvement, audience, locale}, with rationale, source (classifier vs staff) and date; projected into the run context; learning_settings.sector becomes the category key.
5. A product line may override involvement only (productLines[].involvement), chosen by the run input. Archetype, category and locale are per account.
6. A category with no pack opens a stub pack from the onboarding research. Adding a value to archetype, involvement, audience or locale requires a registry PR approved by Albert.
7. Reclassification is by staff action only, logged with who and why, and recompiles the DNA showing which keys changed. Performance never reclassifies a client; it adjusts L3 weights. Review the picks when price, business model or primary offer changes.
recommended.how_guidance_composes:
compileDNA(client, run) at dispatch, pure, no model call, one resolved parameter set plus a provenance map (layer and document version per key) stored on the run.
Merge order: (1) L1 defaults for every registry key; (2) the three facet cards as a plain union, no precedence between them because keys have single owners, a double-write is a CI error not a runtime conflict; (3) the audience modifier on its two keys; (4) locale variants resolved on any value that has them: exact locale, base language, default; (5) L3 DNA overrides (reason required, non-hard keys only), then L3 learned weights (post-job mix, format weights) shrunk toward L1 global; (6) run input: post job, product line; (7) result checked against L1 hard gates.
Conflict rules: hard rules form a floor no later layer can lower: platform constraints (L1), audio source (archetype), compliance and claims values (category pack plus locale jurisdiction, checked by the L1 gate), forbidden topics and brand-kit assets (L3), and product rules (draft-only, never narrate review). Among soft defaults the narrower layer wins: run input > L3 > facets > L1. Where a value genuinely depends on two facets, the registry names one owner; the other facet may influence it only through an interaction table, and interaction tables are permitted only for a cross-grouping that has passed the skill gate (today none, every cross is negative). Literature matching rules (appeal to motive, register to involvement) are DEFAULTS never MUST, per Loef et al.; L3 keeps roughly 1 post in 10 as a logged counter-type experiment. Every L3-over-L2 override is logged and reviewed quarterly so defaults that are often overturned get demoted.
recommended.how_evidence_pools:
Replication and scale tests for performance claims pool GLOBALLY: all benchmark accounts, one vote per account, sign test or interval on the within-account best-minus-weakest difference, false-discovery control, confirmation on fresh posts. A claim that passes becomes an L1 default. L3 (the client's own posts) shrinks toward that global estimate with no facet in between.
No facet pools performance evidence today. Not involvement (+0.0028 is a 0.3% error reduction at the floor of the permutation test), not archetype (-0.0037), and never category, industry, vertical, locale, size or any cross (all negative; locale p=0.51).
SKILL GATE for a facet to earn shrunk pattern deltas on top of L1: on the refreshed corpus, leave-one-account-out skill >= +0.01 with perm_p < 0.05 on two consecutive predictive-test runs; at least 20 accounts in every group used; k tuned by cross-validation rather than fixed at 3; the effect survives dropping any one source client's competitor set (guards the industry-equals-client confound); and the pattern also wins in the L3 data of >= 2 Karos clients in that group. Even then deltas are additive on L1, shrunk n/(n+k) with n in accounts not posts, tagged with the evidence id, and demotable when a later run fails the gate. The owner's '2 clients' rung is a candidate generator for the gate, not a promotion on its own.
Standards enter L2 without engagement proof when they are categorical by nature: law, category entry points, calendar, platform account-type constraints.
Benchmark accounts serve category packs as content inventory (topics, lingo, visual subjects, calendar moments, proof types) and reporting baselines, never as effect sizes.
The predictive test is re-run after every research storm, or when the benchmark grows 25% or more, and published as a leaderboard; involvement and archetype are the watch facets, and each storm's scraping should aim to add accounts to thin groups (place, person, institution, he, pt-BR).
recommended.documents_to_maintain:
1. docs/content-layers.md (engine repo, pointer from the portal's docs/agent-architecture.md): the stack, closed lists and definitions, the three-question involvement rule, tie-breaks, merge order, and the standard-vs-performance-claim definition.
2. facet-registry.json: every parameter key, its single owner, hard or default, allowed values; CI enforces one owner per key, closed vocabularies, and rejects L2 lines tagged as performance claims.
3. facet-archetype.json: one 7-row table, at most ~10 keys per row plus up to 5 one-line prose lines each.
4. ig-kit-<category>/: one category pack per field (7 today), each under ~25 lines: compliance values per jurisdiction key, 8-15 CEPs, calendar, proof conventions, lingo, imagery source, visual conventions, benchmark peer list and baselines. Tone and format-lead lines are removed from the kits (they belong to involvement and archetype); the IG agent prompts that read tone from a kit get a migration.
5. facet-involvement.json: 3 rows (none/low/high: post-job mix, brand-vs-activation ratio, CTA intensity, register, format lead) plus the audience-modifier deltas on its two keys.
6. facet-locale.json: en, he, pt-BR, es, fr, multi with language mechanics and jurisdiction key.
7. ig-dna-<slug>: one per client: classification record (five picks, rationale, source, date, product-line overrides), brand-kit pointers, appeal lean, overrides with reasons, at most 15 client lines, learned weights.
8. Benchmark account register: 89 rows with source client, the five facet tags and the descriptive tags, using the same definitions as clients.
9. evidence/facet-skill-leaderboard.{json,md}: append-only, one entry per predictive-test run (the table above is entry #1), plus every promotion or demotion of a pattern between L1 and a facet with its evidence id. The only input that can unlock a facet's performance priors.
10. Override log: L3-over-L2 overrides and per-run involvement overrides, reviewed quarterly.
Owners: Albert approves the registry, L1 and any MUST; Anna approves category packs and DNAs in her weekly review; the auditor skill writes proposals as pull requests. Roughly 20 small files in total; the facet tables are one file each, not one per value.
recommended.why_this_fits_the_evidence:
The predictive test says the middle layer is not where performance knowledge lives: 15 of 16 groupings predict worse than the global pool, the single positive is 0.3%, crossings are uniformly worse than their parents, and locale is noise. So this design puts every performance claim in L1 (global, one vote per account) and L3 (client, shrunk to global) and nothing in between, which is Design 3's rule and the only one of the three that does not overclaim on +0.0028. It keeps a gate so involvement, the one facet with positive skill and the largest groups, can earn deltas later on evidence rather than on hope, and calibrates that gate (+0.01, two runs, 20 per group, robust to dropping a source client, k by CV) to what an 89-to-150 account benchmark can actually reach, unlike Design 3's 0.02.
What the middle layer DOES own is what the test does not measure and what the literature says is genuinely facet-level: compliance and category entry points and calendar are category-level by law and by Ehrenberg-Bass; voice, face and audio are account-type level by Instagram's own product split (a DJ and a nightclub share a category, not a voice); mix, register and CTA defaults follow the decision type by FCB, Rossiter-Percy and Binet & Field, and can differ inside one category (the two intimates clients). Single-owner keys (Design 2's ownership table, Design 3's registry) mean the facets never need a precedence order, so no fourth stacked layer and no crossed 'segment' keys, which the test shows lose most. B2B is a two-key modifier because the effectiveness evidence says emotion works in B2B too. Rules that held across 782 firms (blend personality and informative, questions draw comments) sit in L1. Locale is a rendering qualifier because p=0.51.
It answers the owner's question directly: the middle is 'what kind of account and what kind of decision' (closed, small, authored) plus 'what the content is about' (category, open, authored). Industries do not decide behaviour; they supply knowledge through kits. It generalises to a category Karos has never served (archetype, involvement, audience, locale are closed picks on day one; only the pack is new work), it is cheap (one small model call at onboarding, none at run time, ~20 files, one offline script per storm), and it keeps the agent-engine pieces already judged good: L1 prompts and gates, mechanism/value split, kits as parameter sets, DNA per client, one vote per account, pure compile with provenance.
risks: 'No grouping predicts' may partly be sample size and confounding rather than absence of an effect: 89 accounts from 7 client-shaped clusters, 66 English, industry equals source client, he and pt-BR each nested in one industry. Mitigation: the leaderboard re-runs every storm and scraping targets thin groups; the gate is explicit so a real facet effect can surface.

The gate itself is a judgment call. +0.01 over two runs may still be reachable by noise on a small benchmark, or may be unreachable if the true effects are around 0.003. Tune k by cross-validation before the second run, and treat the first facet promotion as an experiment with a kill switch (one config flag back to L1-only).

Outcome mismatch: the test measures within-account engagement share, not reach, clicks, leads or sales. The three high-involvement clients (karoslabs, thepitchbydeel, xodigital) care about downstream actions the benchmark cannot see, and involvement may matter most exactly there.

Standards-only packs will drift toward 'what works' lines unless CI actually rejects L2 lines tagged as performance claims and the auditor tags claims reliably. Without that lint the tested-bad axes carry pattern rules again through the side door.

Boundary classifications (hankypanky low vs high, sitti and xodigital platform vs neighbour, dontechno publisher vs person, geektime mixed vs B2B) shift mix and register defaults. Mitigation: neighbouring archetype rows share values on the keys that matter most, product-line override for involvement, staff confirmation, override log; and the benchmark register must use the identical three-question rule or the facet signal erodes.

Identical L2 stacks for same-category same-involvement clients (hankypanky and kindlyyours) put all differentiation on L3 DNA; thin DNA means convergent output. Onboarding must fill positioning, appeal lean and distinctive assets before the first run.

Migration cost: tone and format-lead lines leave the kits, learning_settings.sector becomes a category key with new facet columns, and IG prompts that read tone from a kit must be re-pointed; until both stores carry the same facets the engine docs and the middleware can drift.

The cross-client synthesis, skeptic check, categorization study and layer auditors of the underlying study never completed. This recommendation rests on the predictive test and the literature review; those checks could move the archetype list or the involvement boundaries and should run before the registry is frozen.

verdict.preconditions_for_more_layers: Before any facet (or a new layer) is allowed to carry pooled performance deltas, all of the following must be true and recorded in the leaderboard: (1) the benchmark has been refreshed and broadened so that every group used has at least 20 accounts and at least one facet value is populated by more than one source client (breaks the industry-equals-client and locale-nested-in-industry confounds); (2) the shrinkage k has been tuned by leave-one-account-out cross-validation rather than fixed at 3, and the grouping still shows skill >= +0.01 with perm_p < 0.05 under the tuned k; (3) that result holds on two consecutive predictive-test runs, and survives dropping any single source client's competitor set; (4) the pattern in question also wins in the L3 data of at least 2 Karos clients inside that group; (5) the test has been repeated on at least one outcome besides within-account engagement share (reach, saves, link clicks or lead events) for the high-involvement group, since that is where the facet would matter most; (6) the outstanding study checks (cross-client synthesis, skeptic check, categorization study, layer auditors) have run and do not contradict the closed lists; (7) a demotion path exists: the facet deltas are additive on L1, tagged with an evidence id, and drop back to L1-only by one config flag when a later run fails the gate. A fourth STACKED layer (as opposed to a facet card) needs one further condition: a crossed grouping must beat both of its parent facets on skill, which no cross did at 13-22 cells, and that is not expected until the benchmark reaches roughly 20 accounts per cell.
